Read @fig-constraint-tree one branch at a time, starting from what the defense does wrong.

**(1) Linebackers flow hard: the bootleg.** Outside zone punishes slow linebackers; a linebacker who doesn't
beat his blocker to the play side gets sealed inside and the back runs past him. So linebackers learn to fly.
The bootleg fakes outside zone one way and rolls the quarterback out the other way, behind a blocker
(a pulling guard or the fullback) who takes care of the defensive end on that side; that blocker is why
[04-05](../04-the-passing-game/04-05-play-action-boots-screens.qmd) also called it the *protected boot*. Receivers cross the field
to meet him at three depths, and the crossing routes come open *behind* the linebackers who just ran the
other way. The defense's lesson ("flow fast") is the very thing the bootleg cashes in.

**(2) The backside end chases: the naked boot.** On outside zone, the defensive end on the far side (the
*backside*) has two jobs that pull against each other. He is the man who stops the cutback: if he stays put, the
back has a lane back to his side. But he is also the last defender on that edge, so his coaching, which you met in
[03-05](../03-the-run-game/03-05-perimeter-and-misdirection.qmd), is to **squeeze** while checking *boot, counter,
reverse*: shuffle down the line a yard or two to shrink the cutback lane, keep his shoulders square and his eyes on
the quarterback, and stay at the edge until he is sure the ball has gone the other way. That is the disciplined
version, and it is hard to play. When the cutback has been hurting the defense, the end starts to **crash**
instead: he turns his shoulders, flattens down the line and chases the back. @fig-end-two-ways shows the
difference. Crashing is the cheat. The naked bootleg sends the quarterback right at the spot the crashing end just
left, with *no* blocker for him (that's the "naked"). The end who crashed is now behind a quarterback who is running
away from him, and nobody else is close. If the end squeezed and stayed home instead, he is standing on the
quarterback's launch point, and the quarterback is in trouble, which is the price of a play that only works against
a cheat.

```{python}
#| label: fig-end-two-ways
#| fig-cap: "Two ways to play the backside end (E, red ring) against outside zone right, at the moment the quarterback (Q) would start a naked boot to the left. Left, he squeezes: he shuffles a yard or two down the line with his shoulders square and his eyes on the quarterback (his checklist is boot, counter, reverse), so he is still at the edge, right on the spot the quarterback wants to roll to. Right, he crashes: he turns and chases the back flat down the line, which stops the cutback but leaves him inside and behind the quarterback. The naked boot beats the crash and dies against the squeeze."
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.6, 3.5))
E0 = (1.0, technique("5", -1))                      # the end's alignment, a 5-technique
for ax, crash in zip(axes, (False, True)):
    e1 = (-2.2, 3.3) if crash else (0.4, -2.9)     # where he is when Q would start the boot
    dfn = shifted([q for q in base_43() if q.key not in ("LCB", "RCB", "SS", "FS")], WDE=e1)
    p = Play(offset_i(), dfn, los=35, to_go=None)
    oz_first_second(p, fake=True)
    go_to(p, "QB", (-5.8, -6.8), "run", via=[(-3.6, -1.8)], delay=0.1)
    p.highlight("WDE", color=RED)
    f = draw(p, ax=ax, lateral=(-13.0, 6.5), window=(-8.6, 6.4))
    # where he started: a faint outline and a dashed arrow to where he is now
    was_here(f, p, *E0)
    ghost(f, p, [E0, (E0[0] - 0.2, E0[1] + 0.9), e1] if crash else [E0, e1], alpha=0.9, lw=1.5)
    panel_title(ax, "He crashes: the naked boot wins" if crash else "He squeezes: the naked boot dies", fontsize=8.2)
    if crash:
        point_to(f, p, (4.3, -8.8), e1, "turned and\nchased R: inside,\nbehind Q", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK)
        say(f, p, -7.4, -3.6, "nobody here", fontsize=6.6, color=style.OFFENSE_DARK)
    else:
        point_to(f, p, (4.3, -8.8), e1, "a yard down\nthe line, shoulders\nsquare, eyes on Q", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK)
        say(f, p, -7.4, -3.6, "Q rolls right at E", fontsize=6.6, color=style.DEFENSE_DARK)
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=0.8)
plt.show()
```

**The keeper off the naked.** Once the quarterback is outside with the ball, somebody on that side has to
cover the receivers coming across, and somebody has to stop the quarterback from running. If the defender on
that edge runs with the flat route, the quarterback keeps it and runs, often for a first down, because the
rest of the defense is still on the other side of the field chasing the fake. The keeper is a constraint on a
constraint: it punishes the defense's answer to the naked boot.

**(3) The backside linebacker over-runs: the counter.** The back on outside zone has three choices (bang,
bend, bounce), and the cutback lane is always there for the backside linebacker to fill. If that linebacker
starts running with the flow too, to get to the play side faster, the backside goes empty. The counter starts
exactly like outside zone (the line's first steps, the back's first step) and then brings the ball back the
other way behind a pulling lineman. It's the run version of the bootleg: it punishes everyone who went with
the first step.

**(4) The safety races down: the play-action shot.** A safety in the box is an extra run defender, and against
an outside-zone team the safety on the play side learns to come down fast: a 6-yard run turns into a
2-yard run if he arrives in time. The play-action shot fakes the same run, keeps seven or eight players in to
block, and sends two receivers deep, often in a
[yankee](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-yankee) combination (a post from one side, a deep crosser from the
other). A safety who has come forward for the run can't get back to either.

Notice what the arrows in @fig-constraint-tree all have in common: they start at the *defense*. A constraint
play is defined by the defender it punishes, not by the offense's drawing. That gives you a practical way to
watch: find the defender who is cheating, and you've found the play that's coming.

::: {.callout-note title="Go deeper: the RPO as a built-in constraint"}
The [RPO](../04-the-passing-game/04-06-rpos.qmd) takes this idea to its logical end. Instead of calling the
constraint play on a later snap, after the defense has shown its lean, it attaches the constraint to the base
play *on the same snap*: the line blocks the run, and the quarterback watches one defender (the conflict
defender) and throws behind him if he leans toward the run. The constraint is no longer a separate call that
has to be timed; it's a branch of the base play that fires automatically. That's why RPOs are sometimes
described as "constraint theory in one play." The cost is that the read has to be fast and the pass has to
be short (the ineligible-downfield rule sees to that), so RPOs don't replace the deep constraints, like the
shot play, that punish the safety.
:::

### Same look, four plays: the signature plate

Constraint plays only work if, for the first second, they look like the base play. A linebacker reads a
guard's helmet and the running back's first two steps; if those match what he has seen on every outside zone,
he moves. This is why Shanahan-family offenses are obsessive about *one formation, many plays*: the same
personnel, the same alignment, the same line steps and the same back's track, with the decision about which
play it really is hidden until the defense has already reacted.

In @fig-one-formation-four-plays below, cover the bottom three panels with your hand and look only at the
top-left one. That is what the defense sees for the first half-second of *every* play in the figure: the same
alignment, the same line stepping right (all but one guard, as you'll see), the same back heading toward the
tight end. A defender who
waits to find out which play it is gets beaten by outside zone, because outside zone is a race to the edge. A
defender who reacts at once gets beaten by one of the other three. The offense has made waiting and reacting
both wrong.

How long does a defender have? Not long. A linebacker's read happens in his first step or two, well under a
second, and by the time he is sure, outside zone has already reached the edge. That is why "wait and see" is not
an option for him.

```{python}
#| label: fig-one-formation-four-plays
#| fig-cap: "One formation, four plays (a Shanahan-style plate; illustrative, not a specific team's playbook). Where to look: compare the five linemen's first steps and R's first step across the panels. They match, except for the right guard in C. The offense is identical before the snap in all four panels: 21 personnel, an offset I with the fullback (F) offset to the tight end's side, the receivers in tight splits. A: outside zone right, the base play; the fullback seals the Sam inside and the back presses the tight end's outside leg, then bounces. B: naked boot left: the same line steps and the back's same track without the ball, and F starts on his arc before slicing back to the flat. The quarterback (thick arrow) rolls away from the backside end (red ring, drawn where his chase took him; the dashed outline is where he started), X clears the corner, and the throw (dashed brown) goes to Y crossing underneath. C: counter left: the play-side linemen block down, which is a step to the right, so their first step matches the zone step; the back takes one step right; then the right guard (purple ring) pulls back to kick out the end, and the back cuts inside that block, behind the fullback, who leads onto the Will. The linebackers (red rings) are drawn where they flowed. D: play-action shot: the same fake, seven blockers (the left tackle takes one zone step and hinges back onto the end), a post (X) and a deep crossing route (Z); the free safety (red ring) came down on the fake, so the post is open behind him. For the first half-second the defense sees the same thing four times."
LAT, WIN = (-14, 14), (-9, 20.5)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(6.4, 7.6))
# A. outside zone right
p = Play(offset_i(), base_43(), los=35, to_go=10)
oz_first_second(p)
go_to(p, "Y", (0.3, 5.8)); go_to(p, "FB", (3.0, 6.4), via=[(-2.6, 4.2)])
go_to(p, "RB", (5.0, 7.8), "run", via=[(-5.6, 1.6), (-2.6, 3.8), (0.0, 5.6)])
go_to(p, "Z", (5.0, 9.6)); p.route("X", [(0, 0), (8, 0)])
p.highlight("RB")
f = draw(p, ax=axes[0, 0], lateral=LAT, window=WIN)
panel_title(axes[0, 0], "A. Outside zone right: the base play")
say(f, p, -4.6, -7.0, "line steps right;\nback presses Y's\noutside leg", fontsize=6.6)
# B. naked boot left (the end is drawn where his chase has taken him; the outline shows where he started)
E_CHASE = (-2.6, 3.0)
p = Play(offset_i(), shifted(base_43(), WDE=E_CHASE), los=35, to_go=10)
oz_first_second(p, fake=True)
go_to(p, "QB", (-6.2, -7.4), "run", via=[(-4.2, -2.0)], delay=0.1)
go_to(p, "FB", (2.6, -12.4), "route", via=[(-3.8, 2.4), (-2.8, -2.0), (-1.4, -7.0)], delay=0.2)
p.route("Y", [(0, 0), (1.2, -1.0), (5.0, -5.0), (8.0, -10.0), (8.5, -11.8)])
p.route("Z", [(0, 0), (10, -1.0), (11.5, -11.0), (12.5, -21.5)])
p.route("X", [(0, 0), (18.0, 0.0)])
p.highlight("WDE", color=RED); p.highlight("QB")
p.pass_to("Y", t=4.2)
f = draw(p, ax=axes[0, 1], lateral=LAT, window=WIN)
was_here(f, p, 1.0, technique("5", -1), to=(-1.6, 2.2))
panel_title(axes[0, 1], "B. Naked boot left")
point_to(f, p, (-7.0, 7.4), E_CHASE, "end chased\nthe fake", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK)
say(f, p, 17.0, -6.0, "X clears\nthe corner", fontsize=6.4, color=style.OFFENSE_DARK)
# C. counter left (the linebackers are drawn where their flow has taken them; outlines show where they started)
p = Play(offset_i(), shifted(base_43(), MIKE=(4.4, 3.6), WILL=(4.8, 0.4)), los=35, to_go=10)
go_to(p, "LT", (0.5, -1.5)); go_to(p, "LG", (0.4, -0.4))          # play side blocks down (a step right)
go_to(p, "C", (0.3, 1.9))                                         # back block on the 3-technique
go_to(p, "RT", (0.0, 3.0)); go_to(p, "Y", (0.3, 5.8))             # the back side hinges
go_to(p, "RG", (0.5, -4.4), "pull", via=[(-1.5, 2.0), (-3.0, 0.6), (-2.6, -3.0)])
go_to(p, "FB", (3.8, -0.6), "pull", via=[(-3.8, 1.9), (-3.6, -0.6), (-0.8, -2.8)])
go_to(p, "QB", (-4.1, -0.6), "path", speed=3.0)
go_to(p, "RB", (6.0, -3.2), "run", via=[(-7.0, 1.3), (-4.8, -0.9), (-1.0, -2.9)])
p.highlight("MIKE", "WILL", color=RED); p.highlight("RG", color=PURPLE); p.highlight("RB")
f = draw(p, ax=axes[1, 0], lateral=LAT, window=WIN)
was_here(f, p, 4.6, 1.0); was_here(f, p, 4.6, -2.6)
panel_title(axes[1, 0], "C. Counter left")
point_to(f, p, (12.8, 6.0), (5.2, 3.0), "linebackers\nflowed right", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK)
point_to(f, p, (-4.8, -9.6), (-2.8, -2.0), "RG pulls,\nkicks out E", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK)
# D. play-action shot
p = Play(offset_i(), base_43(), los=35, to_go=10)
oz_first_second(p, fake=True)
go_to(p, "LT", (-1.0, -3.4), via=[(-0.5, -1.8)])                 # one zone step, then hinge back on the end
go_to(p, "QB", (-6.6, -0.6), "path", speed=3.5, delay=0.1)
go_to(p, "Y", (0.3, 5.8)); go_to(p, "FB", (-1.5, 4.8), via=[(-2.8, 4.0)])
p.route("X", [(0, 0), (11.5, 0), (18.0, -7.0)])
p.route("Z", [(0, 0), (9, -0.5), (12.0, -12.0), (13.0, -19.5)])
go_to(p, "FS", (9.0, 1.5), "path"); go_to(p, "SS", (5.0, 5.5), "path")
p.highlight("FS", color=RED)
p.pass_to("X", t=3.0)
f = draw(p, ax=axes[1, 1], lateral=LAT, window=WIN)
panel_title(axes[1, 1], "D. Play-action shot")
point_to(f, p, (17.6, 7.4), (12.6, 0.2), "safety comes\ndown on the fake", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK)
fig.tight_layout(h_pad=0.8, w_pad=0.6)
plt.show()
```

Look closely and the plays aren't *perfectly* identical, which matters for the arms race. On the counter the
right guard pulls left instead of stepping right, a clue for a linebacker disciplined enough to read the guard
instead of the back. On the naked boot nobody blocks the backside end, and that is a louder clue than it sounds:
on a real outside zone somebody, the backside tackle or a tight end, cuts or cuts off that end (the block the
tight end showed and then abandoned on 04-05's naked boot), so a well-coached end's rule is "no cut, no block: think boot." Defenses coach to those clues ("read the guard," "if nobody blocks
you, think boot"), and offenses answer by disguising the clue: the protected boot puts a blocker back on the end,
and some counters pull a tight end instead of a guard. The game never ends; it just moves to smaller details.

### Why not just run the constraint play more?

Here is the puzzle that comes with every constraint play. In
[Perimeter Runs and Misdirection](../03-the-run-game/03-05-perimeter-and-misdirection.qmd) you saw that an NFL
receiver's carry (jet sweeps, end-arounds, reverses) has been worth far more on average than a running back's,
every season from 2016 to 2025. In
[Play-Action, Bootlegs, and Screens](../04-the-passing-game/04-05-play-action-boots-screens.qmd) you saw that
play-action dropbacks beat ordinary dropbacks by a wide margin, season after season. If the constraint plays
are that much better, aren't coaches leaving points on the table by calling them so rarely?

Partly, maybe. But a simple model shows why a constraint play *should* look better on average than the base
play even when a coach is calling it exactly the right amount. Imagine the offense chooses what share of its
snaps to spend on the constraint play. As that share rises, the defense sees it more on film and respects it
more: it cheats less against the base play. So the constraint play gets worse the more it's called (fewer
defenders are cheating for it to punish) and the base play gets better (fewer defenders are cheating against
it).

```{python}
#| label: fig-dose-model
#| fig-cap: "A toy model of the dose (made-up numbers chosen to make the shape visible, not estimates). As the offense calls the constraint play more often, the defense respects it more: the constraint play's value per snap falls (orange) and the base play's rises a little (blue). The offense's average over all its snaps (dashed) peaks, at the dot, well before the two lines cross. At that best mix the constraint play is still worth more per snap than the base play (the bracket), yet calling it more would lower the average, because each extra call makes the defense respect it more on every snap, base plays included."
style.apply()
A_C, S_C, A_B, S_B = 0.60, 3.0, 0.02, 0.30          # constraint and base play: value = intercept + slope x share
q = np.linspace(0, 0.30, 301)
C = A_C - S_C * q
B = A_B + S_B * q
V = q * C + (1 - q) * B
qs = round(float(q[np.argmax(V)]), 2)
Cs, Bs, Vs = A_C - S_C * qs, A_B + S_B * qs, qs * (A_C - S_C * qs) + (1 - qs) * (A_B + S_B * qs)
# the worked example: move one more percentage point of snaps from the base play to the constraint play
GAIN = 0.01 * (Cs - Bs)                 # the extra constraint call is worth more than the base call it replaces
COST = qs * S_C * 0.01                  # ... but every constraint call already being made loses a little
LIFT = (1 - qs) * S_B * 0.01            # ... and every base call gains a little
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.4, 3.5))
ax.axhline(0, color=style.BASELINE, lw=0.9)
ax.plot(q * 100, C, color=style.SERIES[1], lw=2, label="constraint play (e.g. the bootleg)")
ax.plot(q * 100, B, color=style.SERIES[0], lw=2, label="base play (e.g. outside zone)")
ax.plot(q * 100, V, color=style.INK, lw=1.6, ls=(0, (4, 2)), label="offense's average over all snaps")
ax.plot([qs * 100], [Vs], "o", color=style.INK, ms=6, zorder=5)
ax.axvline(qs * 100, color=style.MUTED, lw=0.9, zorder=0)
ax.annotate("", (qs * 100 + 0.5, Cs), (qs * 100 + 0.5, Bs),
            arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="<->", color=style.INK, lw=1.4))
ax.annotate("at the best mix, the constraint\nplay still looks better per snap",
            (qs * 100 + 0.7, (Cs + Bs) / 2), xytext=(19.0, 0.36), fontsize=7.5, color=style.INK,
            ha="left", va="center", arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-", color=style.INK_2, lw=0.7))
ax.annotate(f"the average peaks here,\nabout {qs:.0%} of snaps", (qs * 100, Vs), xytext=(19.0, -0.08),
            fontsize=7.5, color=style.INK, ha="left", va="center",
            arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-", color=style.INK_2, lw=0.7))
ax.set_xlabel("share of snaps spent on the constraint play (%)", fontsize=8)
ax.set_ylabel("EPA per snap (illustrative)", fontsize=8)
ax.tick_params(labelsize=7.5)
ax.set_xlim(0, 30); ax.set_ylim(-0.32, 0.65)
ax.legend(loc="lower left", bbox_to_anchor=(0.0, 0.0), fontsize=7.5, frameon=False)
ax.set_title("Why a constraint play's average flatters it", fontsize=10)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

The dashed line in @fig-dose-model is what the offense actually cares about: its expected points per snap,
counting every snap. It peaks at about `{python} f"{qs:.0%}"` here, and at that peak the constraint play is
still worth clearly more per snap than the base play. Why stop there? Work through what one more percentage point
of constraint calls would do, with the toy numbers at the peak:

- **The gain.** One snap in a hundred switches from the base play (worth `{python} f"{Bs:+.2f}"`) to the constraint
  play (worth `{python} f"{Cs:+.2f}"`). That adds `{python} f"{GAIN:+.4f}"` EPA per snap, averaged over all snaps.
- **The cost.** The defense, seeing the constraint a little more often, respects it a little more. Every
  constraint call the offense was *already* making (`{python} f"{qs:.0%}"` of snaps) loses about
  `{python} f"{0.01 * S_C:.2f}"`: `{python} f"{-COST:+.4f}"` per snap.
- **The side benefit.** A defense respecting the constraint more cheats less against the base play, so every base
  call gains about `{python} f"{0.01 * S_B:.3f}"`: `{python} f"{LIFT:+.4f}"` per snap.

Add them up and the net is roughly zero. That is what "the peak" means: the value of *one more* call (economists say
"at the margin") has fallen to nothing, even though the *average* constraint call is still worth far more than the
average base call. The constraint play's average includes all the early, profitable calls; the next call only gets
the margin.

So "the constraint play averages more than the base play" is not, by itself, evidence that coaches are under-using
it; a well-run offense *should* show exactly that gap.[^minimax] What the gap can't tell you is whether a
particular team is at its peak or short of it, and economists who study play-calling have argued both
ways. A second reason the gap flatters constraint plays is selection: coaches call them when they see the
defense leaning, so their average is built from good moments. That's not cheating the numbers. That's the job.

## The illusion of complexity

Constraint theory says the plays must look alike. Turn that into a design principle for a whole offense and you
get what coaches call the **[illusion of complexity](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-illusion-of-complexity)**:
make a few plays look like many, and many plays look like one, so that the defense has to prepare for far more
than the offense has to learn.[^illusion] It has two halves, and you have already seen one of them.

**Many plays, one look.** That's @fig-one-formation-four-plays: four plays from one picture, so the picture
tells the defense nothing.

**One play, many looks.** The other half runs the same play out of different formations, personnel groups and
motions. The linemen's assignments don't change at all; only the costume does.

```{python}
#| label: fig-one-play-four-outfits
#| fig-cap: "One play, four outfits: outside zone right from four different looks (illustrative). In every panel the five linemen take the same first step to the right (the short blocks ending in bars), the back aims at the same spot (the green X, just outside the tight end), and the blocking rules are identical. Only the dressing changes: two backs (21 personnel), three receivers from the shotgun (11), two tight ends with one on a wing (12), and three receivers with Z in motion across the formation away from the play, a decoy to pull defenders' eyes and feet the wrong way. To the offense this is one play to learn. The grey note under each panel is what the defense has to change to match that look: four alignments to install and practice."


def gun_11():
    return line() + [O("QB", "QB", -5.0, 0.0, "Q"), O("RB", "RB", -5.2, -2.4, "R"), O("Y", "TE", -0.7, 4.8, "Y"),
                     O("H", "WR", -1.5, -7.0, "H"), O("X", "WR", -0.7, -10.5, "X"), O("Z", "WR", -1.5, 10.5, "Z")]


def wing_12():
    return line() + [O("QB", "QB", -1.9, 0.0, "Q"), O("RB", "RB", -7.0, 0.0, "R"), O("Y", "TE", -0.7, 4.8, "Y"),
                     O("U", "TE", -1.5, 6.4, "U"), O("X", "WR", -0.7, -9.5, "X"), O("Z", "WR", -1.5, 10.5, "Z")]


def jet_11():
    return line() + [O("QB", "QB", -1.9, 0.0, "Q"), O("RB", "RB", -7.0, 0.0, "R"), O("Y", "TE", -0.7, 4.8, "Y"),
                     O("H", "WR", -1.5, -6.5, "H"), O("X", "WR", -0.7, -10.5, "X"), O("Z", "WR", -1.5, 10.5, "Z")]


OZ_TRACK = [(-5.6, 1.6), (-2.6, 3.8), (0.0, 5.4)]
specs = [("21 personnel, offset I", offset_i(), OZ_TRACK, "defense: base 4-3, eight in the box"),
         ("11 personnel, shotgun", gun_11(), [(-4.2, 0.6), (-2.2, 3.6), (0.0, 5.4)],
          "defense: nickel, a slot corner on H"),
         ("12 personnel, wing right", wing_12(), OZ_TRACK, "defense: base, widen the edge to the wing"),
         ("11 personnel, motion away", jet_11(), OZ_TRACK, "defense: decide who travels with Z")]
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(6.6, 4.6))
for ax, (ttl, off, via, dnote) in zip(axes.flat, specs):
    p = Play(off, [], los=35, to_go=None)
    for k in ("LT", "LG", "C", "RG", "RT"):
        p.block(k, pts=[(0.5, 2.0)])
    go_to(p, "Y", (0.3, 6.2))
    if "FB" in p.players:
        go_to(p, "FB", (2.6, 6.8), via=[(-2.6, 4.2)])
    if "U" in p.players:
        go_to(p, "U", (1.2, 8.0))
    if ttl.endswith("motion away"):
        p.motion("Z", to=(-3.6, -3.0))                 # the ball is snapped once Z has cleared the mesh
        go_to(p, "Z", (-3.8, -10.0), "path", speed=8.0)
    go_to(p, "RB", (3.4, 8.4), "run", via=via)
    p.highlight("RB")
    f = draw(p, ax=ax, lateral=(-12.5, 12.5), window=(-8.6, 4.6))
    sx, sy = _P(f, p, 0.0, 5.6)
    ax.plot([sx], [sy], marker="X", ms=7, color=style.THIRD, mec="white", mew=0.7, zorder=9)
    panel_title(ax, ttl, fontsize=8)
    ax.text(0.5, -0.04, dnote, transform=ax.transAxes, ha="center", va="top", fontsize=7.0, color=style.INK_2,
            style="italic")
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=0.5, h_pad=1.4)
plt.show()
```

Why does this work so well? Because the burden falls unevenly. A defense doesn't line up against a play; it
lines up against a *formation*, with rules for who aligns where against two backs, against three receivers,
against a wing, against motion. Every new look is something the defense has to install, practice and get
right in a few seconds before the snap. The offense, meanwhile, practices one set of blocking rules. In
@fig-one-play-four-outfits the offense learned one play, and the defense had to learn four answers. Multiply
by a game plan's worth of plays and formations and the arithmetic gets lopsided fast: eight formations with three
motions each is 24 pictures the defense must have an alignment for, and behind each picture could be any of a
dozen core plays, so the defense prepares for close to three hundred combinations while the offense still
practices a dozen plays.

The second payoff is that the outfits hide **tells**, the pre-snap clues you met in
[How to Watch a Broadcast](../01-foundations/01-06-how-to-watch-a-broadcast.qmd). If an offense runs outside zone
only from the offset I, the offset I is a tell. Spread the same play over four looks and every look carries
several plays, so none of them gives the play away. This is a big part of why pre-snap motion has spread so
fast: PFF charted a shift or motion on 63.9% of NFL plays in 2025, up from 38.4% in 2016.[^motion] Motion is
cheap dressing. It costs the offense almost nothing to learn and the defense a great deal to handle.

**What it costs.** The illusion has limits. A play still needs the right players to work: outside zone from
an empty backfield is not outside zone. Every new outfit adds a little to the players' memory load and to the
chance of a busted alignment. And the outfits only stay an illusion if the plays inside them are mixed: a
formation used for one play is just a tell with extra steps.

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: Los Angeles Rams 2018"}
Sean McVay's 2018 Rams took the "one look" half of the illusion to an extreme. They used 11 personnel (one back,
one tight end, three receivers) on about 93% of their plays, against a league median of about 65%, by this
book's count from nflverse data.[^rams18] A defense facing them could learn almost nothing from the substitution
before each snap, because there was almost never a substitution: runs, play-action passes and dropbacks all came
from the same eleven players, usually in a tight, condensed alignment, often with a receiver in motion. The
constraint plays in 03-05's film room (the jet sweeps that went for big gains) worked partly because they came
out of the same look as everything else.

**What to notice:** when a team never changes personnel, stop looking at personnel and start looking at the
details inside the look: the back's depth, the receivers' splits, which way the motion goes. That's where a
one-look offense hides, and where it sometimes leaks.
:::

## Sequencing: plays in an order

Constraint theory tells you *which* plays belong together. **[Sequencing](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-sequencing)**
is the order you call them in: show the defense a look, watch how it reacts, then call the play that beats that
reaction. It turns a playbook into a conversation.

The idea is old. The Delaware Wing-T that you met in 03-05 was built as series football, and its coach, Harold
"Tubby" Raymond, put the point bluntly: "The Wing-T is more than a formation. It is sequence football."[^raymond]
In the series the buck sweep comes first; the buck trap, the waggle and the counter are what the offense calls when
the defense starts stopping the sweep. The mechanism is the defense's key. Both guards pull on the buck sweep, so
linebackers learn to read the guards and chase them; the rest of the series starts with the same backfield action
and puts the ball where the chasing linebackers just left: inside on the trap, back the other way on the counter,
and, on the waggle, a bootleg away from the sweep fake. To the linebacker reading the backfield, the constraint looks
like the base play, which is the whole idea. Bill Walsh's habit of scripting his first fifteen or so plays (the
[opening script](08-03-game-planning-week.qmd) that the next chapter takes apart) was partly a sequencing tool
too: he planned in advance which looks to show early so he could see how the defense answered them and call the
answers later.[^walsh]

Sequencing comes in three shapes you can watch for.

**1. Setting up the counter.** Run the base play until the defense flows hard to it, then call the play that goes
back against the flow. You don't call the counter because the counter is good; you call it because the defense's
last three reactions say it will be.

```{python}
#| label: fig-counter-strip
#| fig-cap: "The counter, after the defense has learned to flow (simulated, BDB-format tracking; faint lines are each player's path so far). The offense shows the outside-zone look from earlier in the game. (1) Every lineman, the right guard included, takes his first step to the right, and the back (green ring) steps right with them; the linebackers, trained by the earlier outside-zone runs, start to flow. (2) The back takes the handoff going left as the right guard and the fullback (purple rings) pull back across. (3) The guard kicks out the end on the left (the backside end of the zone fake, but the play-side end of the counter); the back cuts inside that block, the fullback leads through the hole, and the Will, who flowed, is a step late coming back. (4) The back is through the line on the side the linebackers just left."
def counter_play():
    p = Play(offset_i(labels=True), base_43(), los=35, to_go=None)
    # offense: the line's first steps look like outside zone right
    for k, e in (("LT", (0.6, -1.5)), ("LG", (0.5, -0.3)), ("C", (0.4, 1.0))):
        go_to(p, k, e, speed=1.6)
    go_to(p, "RT", (0.1, 3.6), speed=1.6); go_to(p, "Y", (0.4, 5.6), speed=1.8)
    go_to(p, "RG", (-0.5, 2.1), "block", speed=1.6)                 # the same first step as everyone else ...
    go_to(p, "RG", (0.1, -4.6), "pull", via=[(-1.5, 1.6), (-1.5, -2.8)], speed=5.5)   # ... then the pull
    go_to(p, "FB", (3.0, -1.4), "pull", via=[(-3.6, 0.2), (-3.3, -2.2), (0.2, -2.6)], speed=5.6, delay=0.35)
    go_to(p, "QB", (-2.7, 0.7), "path", speed=2.4)                 # opens to the right, like zone ...
    go_to(p, "QB", (-4.3, -0.4), "path", speed=2.6, delay=0.1)     # ... then turns back to meet the back
    go_to(p, "RB", (-7.0, 1.6), "run", speed=3.2)                  # one step with the zone flow
    go_to(p, "RB", (7.0, -3.4), "run", delay=0.15, speed=6.6, via=[(-4.6, -0.7), (-1.2, -3.0), (2.0, -3.1)])
    p.handoff("RB", t=1.17)
    # defense: the linebackers flow right with the line
    go_to(p, "MIKE", (3.9, 4.2), "path", speed=4.6); go_to(p, "WILL", (4.0, 1.6), "path", speed=4.6)
    go_to(p, "WILL", (3.0, -0.8), "path", speed=3.5, delay=0.1)
    go_to(p, "SAM", (3.0, 7.5), "path", speed=3.0)
    go_to(p, "WDE", (1.2, -4.2), "path", speed=1.0); go_to(p, "WDE", (0.6, -5.6), "path", speed=1.5, delay=0.2)
    go_to(p, "WDT", (1.0, 0.3), "path", speed=1.0); go_to(p, "SDT", (1.0, 3.2), "path", speed=1.0)
    go_to(p, "SDE", (1.2, 6.6), "path", speed=1.0)
    go_to(p, "SS", (6.0, 6.2), "path", speed=3.0); go_to(p, "FS", (10.0, -2.5), "path", speed=3.5, delay=0.6)
    return p


animation_or_strip(counter_play(), [0.3, 1.2, 1.8, 2.8],
                   ["every lineman, RG included, and R\nstep right; the linebackers start to flow",
                    "handoff going left; RG and F\npull back across",
                    "RG kicks out the end; F leads\nthrough; the Will is a step late",
                    "R is through the hole; the flow\nis on the wrong side"],
                   lateral=(-9.5, 9.5), window=(-8.5, 9.0),
                   rings=(("RB", style.THIRD), ("RG", PURPLE), ("FB", PURPLE)))
```

**2. Play-action off the base run.** After the base run has gained yards from a look, call play-action from the
same look within the next few snaps. This is the most common sequence in football, and the most watchable,
because you can see it coming. Notice what [04-05](../04-the-passing-game/04-05-play-action-boots-screens.qmd)
showed, though: linebackers bite on a good fake whether or not the run has been working. So coaches describe the
sequence as being less about "earning" the fake with yards than about *timing*: a defense that has just been
gashed is primed to come forward hard, its coaches have just told it to, and the offense knows that.

Is there any sign of that in the data? A little. On neutral first-and-10 snaps from 2022 to 2025, play-action
passes called right after a run of 10 or more yards on the same drive averaged
`{python} f"{AFTER.loc[True, 'mean']:+.2f}"` EPA, against `{python} f"{AFTER.loc[False, 'mean']:+.2f}"` for
play-action at other times, and the gap showed up in `{python} AFTER_SEASONS` of the 4 seasons. Offenses did not
call much *more* play-action at those moments (`{python} pct(AFTER_SHARE[True])` of dropbacks, against
`{python} pct(AFTER_SHARE[False])`), and the sample is small (`{python} f"{int(AFTER.loc[True, 'size']):,}"`
snaps, so the gap is under two standard errors), so read it as consistent with the coaches' timing story
rather than as proof of it.[^afterrun]

**3. The tendency breaker.** The third shape needs two new words. A
**[tendency](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-tendency)** is a pattern in what a team does in a given situation,
formation or personnel group (running on four snaps in five from one look, throwing to the tight end on most
third-and-shorts) that an opponent can find on film or in data and play against. A
**[tendency breaker](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-tendency-breaker)** is a play called *on purpose* against
your own tendency: a pass from the run look, a run from the empty backfield, a screen from the formation you
always use for deep shots. It punishes an opponent who studied you, and it keeps the pattern honest for next week.

Put the three together and a drive starts to read like a conversation. Here is an illustrative one (not a real
drive), with the defense's side of the conversation in the last column:

| Snap | Situation | The look | The call | What the defense learned |
|----|--------------|----------------|------------------|-----------------------------------|
| 1 | 1st and 10, own 25 | 21 personnel, offset I | Outside zone right: +5 | "This look means outside zone." |
| 3 | 1st and 10, own 36 | Same look | Outside zone right: +7 | Linebackers start flowing on the first step. |
| 4 | 2nd and 3, own 43 | Same look | Counter left: +11 | "Don't over-run; the back side has to fill the cutback." |
| 6 | 2nd and 4, opp. 40 | Same look | Outside zone right: +5 | Backside end starts crashing down the line to stop the cutback. |
| 7 | 1st and 10, opp. 35 | Same look | Naked boot left: +19 | Too late. |

(Snaps 2 and 5, a 6-yard gain each, came from other looks.) The offense ran one look five times and called three
plays, and the order did the work. Snaps 1 and 3 taught the linebackers to flow, so snap 4's counter went back
against them. The counter taught the defense that the cutback side needed help, so on snap 6 the backside end
stopped squeezing and started crashing down the line to take the cutback away, and that crashing end is exactly the
man the naked boot on snap 7 is built to beat. Real defenses adjust like this between series, usually because a
coach in the booth or on the sideline tablet tells them to; how that works in real time is in
[In-Game Adjustments](08-04-in-game-adjustments-and-tempo.qmd).

::: {.callout-caution title="Common misconception"}
"A balanced offense alternates run and pass." Alternating is a pattern too, and patterns are what defenses
hunt. An economic study of NFL play-calling found that teams were *more* likely to switch between run and
pass from one play to the next than a truly unpredictable mix would be, which makes the next call easier to
guess, not harder.[^levitt] Balance means the defense can't tell from the look or the last play what comes
next, not that the offense takes turns.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: Kansas City Chiefs, Super Bowl LVII (2022 season)"}
Andy Reid's offense is famous for the second half of the illusion of complexity, a huge menu of formations,
shifts and motions dressing a stable core of concepts, and for sequencing that plays on what a defense did a few
minutes earlier. The best-known example is the pair of fourth-quarter touchdowns in Super Bowl LVII against the
Eagles, built on a return-motion play the team called "Corn Dog" (the full story is in
[Motion and Shifts](../02-personnel-and-formations/02-06-motion-and-shifts.qmd)): Kadarius Toney scored on it,
and less than three minutes of game clock later Skyy Moore scored on a mirrored version to the other side. Both
times the Eagles' man defender went with the motion and the receiver was alone when he turned back.[^corndog]

**What to notice:** the second call was the same play. Sequencing doesn't always mean switching to a
constraint. If the defense hasn't fixed what beat it, the right next call is the same question again, and
a staff that's watching closely knows when a defense hasn't adjusted. A year later, in Super Bowl LVIII, a
renamed relative of the play produced the winning overtime touchdown: same idea, new clothes.
:::

## Tendencies and the self-scout

Every play an offense calls goes on film, and every opponent's quality control coaches (the entry-level
assistants from [01-04](../01-foundations/01-04-what-a-play-really-is.qmd) who break film down into numbers)
log it: down, distance, field position, personnel, formation, motion, run or pass, direction, result. From
those logs come the tendencies a defense plays against on Sunday. A defense that knows an offense runs 80% of
the time from a particular look can set its front, its linebackers' keys and its safety's depth to stop the run
before the snap, and be right four times in five.

So offenses do the same thing to themselves. A **[self-scout](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-self-scout)** is
a team's study of its own film and data, the way an opponent would study it, to find the tendencies it is giving
away. Many teams do a formal one during the bye week, and the same questions come up in smaller ways all
season.[^selfscout] The questions are the opponent's
questions: What do we do from each personnel group and formation? Which way do we run when the back is offset
left? What do we do after a motion? What do we call on second-and-long after a first-down run? Where are we a
coin flip, and where are we a giveaway?

What a team does with the answers is a judgment call, and there are three choices:

- **Break it.** Call a few tendency breakers from the giveaway look, so the next opponent's numbers are muddier.
- **Hide it.** Spread the giveaway play across more outfits (the illusion of complexity again) so no single look
  carries it.
- **Keep it as bait.** Leave the tendency in place on purpose, let the opponent load up for it, and save the
  breaker for the moment it will hurt most: a big third down, the red zone, the playoffs.

### Building a tendency table

You can run the opponent's first question yourself. A *tendency table* cross-tabulates two things a defense
can see before the snap (here, the offense's personnel group and the quarterback's alignment) and shows how
often each combination produced a pass. Why the quarterback's alignment and not the formation? Because it is the
only formation information in the public data: nflverse records whether the quarterback was under center, in the
shotgun or in the pistol, but not the receivers' splits or the backfield set. A real tendency report charts far more:
dozens of formation codes (2x2, 3x1, bunch, nub), the back's offset, the motion and its direction, the hash and the
field zone ("runs to the field," "runs to the tight end," "runs to the side the back is offset"). So whatever this
table finds is a *floor* on what a pro staff gets from the look. To keep the situation from doing the talking (everyone throws on
third-and-long), the table uses only *neutral* snaps: first and second down, the game reasonably close, outside
the last two minutes of each half. The formal version of this filter, and expected-pass models that adjust for
the situation play by play, are in [Tendencies, PROE and Charting](../13-analytics-and-data/13-04-tendencies-proe-and-charting.qmd).[^neutral]

The recipe, if you want to build one yourself (the code is under "Show the Python" on the website): load a season's
play-by-play with nflreadpy; join the participation file for personnel and the FTN charting file for the
quarterback's alignment, matching on game and play; keep the neutral first- and second-down snaps; then make a
pivot table of the `pass` flag's mean by personnel group and alignment, with a second pivot of counts so you can
ignore cells with only a handful of snaps.

```{python}
#| label: fig-tendency-table
#| fig-cap: "A tendency table: how often the offense passed, by personnel group (rows) and quarterback alignment (columns), neutral situations of the 2024 regular season (first and second down, win probability 20–80%, outside the last two minutes of each half). Left, the Detroit Lions in Ben Johnson's last season as their offensive coordinator; right, all 32 teams together. Blue cells lean pass, orange cells lean run, pale cells are close to a coin flip; grey cells had fewer than 15 snaps. League-wide, the quarterback's alignment is a loud tell: about seven passes in ten from the shotgun, three in ten from under center, two to three in ten from the pistol. The Lions were much closer to even under center. Data: nflverse play-by-play, participation (personnel) and FTN charting (alignment) via nflreadpy."
cmap = LinearSegmentedColormap.from_list("run_pass", [style.SERIES[1], style.DIVERGING[1], style.SERIES[0]])
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.6, 2.9), sharey=True)
for ax, (rt, nn, ttl) in zip(axes, [(R_DET, N_DET, "Detroit Lions, 2024"), (R_NFL, N_NFL, "All 32 teams, 2024")]):
    vals = np.where(nn.values >= 15, rt.values, np.nan)
    ax.imshow(vals, cmap=cmap, vmin=0, vmax=1, aspect="auto")
    for i in range(vals.shape[0]):
        for j in range(vals.shape[1]):
            if nn.values[i, j] >= 15:
                ax.text(j, i - 0.12, f"{rt.values[i, j]:.0%}", ha="center", va="center", fontsize=9.5,
                        fontweight="bold", color=style.INK)
                ax.text(j, i + 0.24, f"n={int(nn.values[i, j]):,}", ha="center", va="center", fontsize=6.6,
                        color=style.INK_2)
            else:
                ax.add_patch(plt.Rectangle((j - 0.5, i - 0.5), 1, 1, fc=style.GRID, ec="none"))
                ax.text(j, i, "too few" if nn.values[i, j] else "none", ha="center", va="center", fontsize=6.6,
                        color=style.MUTED)
    ax.set_xticks(range(3), rt.columns, fontsize=7.6)
    ax.set_yticks(range(len(rt)), [f"{g} personnel" for g in rt.index], fontsize=7.6)
    ax.tick_params(length=0)
    for sp in ax.spines.values():
        sp.set_visible(False)
    ax.set_xticks(np.arange(-0.5, 3, 1), minor=True); ax.set_yticks(np.arange(-0.5, len(rt), 1), minor=True)
    ax.grid(False); ax.grid(which="minor", color=style.SURFACE, lw=2.5); ax.tick_params(which="minor", length=0)
    ax.set_title(ttl, fontsize=9.5)
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=1.0)
plt.show()
```

The right-hand table in @fig-tendency-table is the league's starting point, and the loudest thing in it is not
personnel at all: it's where the quarterback stands. From the shotgun, offenses passed on about seven neutral
snaps in ten; from under center, about three in ten; from the pistol (the quarterback a few yards back with the
back behind him), even fewer. Personnel barely moves those numbers. A defense that saw nothing but the
quarterback's feet would already be well ahead of a coin flip.

Now the Lions. In 2024, Ben Johnson's third and final season calling Detroit's plays, they passed on
`{python} pct(R_DET.loc['11', 'Under center'])` of their neutral 11-personnel snaps from under center, against
`{python} pct(R_NFL.loc['11', 'Under center'])` for the league, and on about four in ten from under center with
two or three tight ends. That's a self-scouted offense: the look that screams "run" for everyone else was close to
much closer to even in Detroit, because Johnson used it for play-action as readily as for runs. The shotgun was more
predictable (`{python} pct(R_DET.loc['12', 'Shotgun'])` passes from 12 personnel), but only on 35 snaps; Detroit
lived under center, where its pictures said the least. (The empty 21-personnel cells don't mean the Lions left the
family. The modern Shanahan-tree offenses mostly hide the same one-look, many-plays idea in 11 and 12 personnel
under center, with a tight end or a receiver doing the fullback's motion and blocking jobs.)

```{python}
#| code-summary: "Show the Python (build any team's tendency table)"
#| eval: false
# Change the team and season to build your own table (seasons 2022-2025 are loaded above).
rate, n = tendency_table(N, team="KC", season=2025, groups=("11", "12", "13"))
print((100 * rate).round(0).astype("Int64"))   # pass rate, %
print(n)                                        # snaps behind each cell: ignore cells with only a handful
```

### How much does the look give away?

A table shows the pattern; the question a defensive coordinator cares about is how much it's *worth*. So run
the scout's experiment honestly. For every neutral snap from 2022 to 2025, predict run or pass using only that
team's *other* games that season (as a scout would, from film he has already seen): if the team passed on more
than half of its snaps from this personnel-and-alignment look elsewhere, guess pass. Compare that with a dumber
guess that ignores the look and uses only the team's overall lean.

League-wide, the overall lean alone called about `{python} pct(ACC_SEASON['hit_team'].mean())` of neutral snaps
correctly, barely better than a coin. (For a team close to 50/50 overall, it can even do *worse* than a coin: if the
team passed on 52% of snaps in its other games but ran more often in this one, every guess in this game is "pass"
and most are wrong.) The look called about `{python} pct(ACC_SEASON['hit_look'].mean())`. Two
pre-snap facts, personnel and where the quarterback stands, turn a coin flip into two right guesses in three.
@fig-look-predictability shows how much that varied by team.

```{python}
#| label: fig-look-predictability
#| fig-cap: "How much each offense's pre-snap look gave away, 2024 and 2025 regular seasons (neutral situations). For each snap, run or pass was predicted from the team's other games that season, using either the team's overall run/pass lean (grey) or the pass rate of that personnel-and-alignment look (blue). Lower blue dots are harder offenses to read. In 2024 the three least predictable offenses by this measure were Green Bay, the Rams and Detroit; for Green Bay the look was no help at all. Teams named in this chapter are in bold. The dark vertical line at 50% is a coin flip. Data: nflverse play-by-play, participation and FTN charting; course calculation."
style.apply()
SHOW = {"GB", "LA", "DET", "CHI", "SF", "MIA", "PHI", "KC"}
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.6, 6.0))
for ax, s in zip(axes, [2024, 2025]):
    a = ACC.loc[s].sort_values("hit_look")
    y = np.arange(len(a))
    ax.hlines(y, a["hit_team"] * 100, a["hit_look"] * 100, color=style.GRID, lw=2.0, zorder=1)
    ax.scatter(a["hit_team"] * 100, y, s=16, color=style.MUTED, zorder=2, label="team's overall\nrun/pass lean")
    ax.scatter(a["hit_look"] * 100, y, s=26, color=style.SERIES[0], zorder=3, edgecolor=style.SURFACE, lw=0.6,
               label="the pre-snap look")
    ax.set_yticks(y, a.index, fontsize=6.4)
    for lab in ax.get_yticklabels():
        if lab.get_text() in SHOW:
            lab.set_fontweight("bold"); lab.set_color(style.INK)
    ax.axvline(50, color=style.INK_2, lw=1.1, zorder=0)
    ax.text(50.4, len(a) - 0.5, "coin flip", fontsize=6.6, color=style.INK_2, ha="left", va="top")
    ax.set_xlim(38, 80); ax.set_ylim(-0.8, len(a) - 0.2)
    ax.grid(axis="y", visible=False)
    ax.set_xlabel("neutral snaps called correctly (%)", fontsize=8)
    ax.tick_params(axis="x", labelsize=7.5)
    ax.set_title(f"{s}", fontsize=10)
axes[0].legend(loc="lower right", fontsize=7, frameon=False, handletextpad=0.3)
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=1.2)
plt.show()
```

The bottom of the 2024 chart reads like a family tree. Matt LaFleur's Packers, Sean McVay's Rams and Johnson's
Lions were the three hardest offenses to read from the look; Green Bay's looks were actually *worse* than useless,
because what the Packers did from a look in one game didn't carry over to the next. In 2025 the Packers were near
the bottom again, along with the Jets (whose looks were also worse than nothing, and whose offensive coordinator
that season, Tanner Engstrand, had been Johnson's passing-game coordinator in Detroit),[^jets] Mike McDaniel's
Dolphins and Johnson's new team in Chicago. Most of the hardest offenses to read share one family of ideas: under-center
outside zone, bootlegs and play-action from shared looks, the Shanahan tree and its close relatives, built around
exactly the idea in @fig-one-formation-four-plays. At the other end, the most predictable offenses let the look
call about three snaps in four for the defense.

Two cautions keep this honest. First, "predictable" is not the same as "bad": a good offense can tell you what's
coming and do it anyway (see the Eagles below), and an unpredictable offense can still be poor at executing. This
chart measures what the look gave away, not what it cost. Across the 128 team-seasons from 2022 to 2025, how well
the look predicted an offense and how many points per play that offense produced were essentially unrelated
(correlation `{python} f"{CORR:+.2f}"`); the fuller version of that question is in
[13-04](../13-analytics-and-data/13-04-tendencies-proe-and-charting.qmd). Second, a team's measure moves from year to year with
its quarterback, its injuries and its coordinator, so read the shape of the chart more than any single rank.

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: Philadelphia Eagles 2024 — a tendency they could afford"}
The 2024 Eagles show the other side of the self-scout. In neutral situations they lined up in the pistol with
11 personnel `{python} PHI_N` times and passed on `{python} pct(PHI_PASS)` of them: about as loud a tell as an
offense gives. They kept it anyway. Saquon Barkley ran for 2,005 yards that season behind one of the league's best
lines, and the Eagles won Super Bowl LIX.[^barkley]

Knowing "run" also didn't tell a defense *which* run. The Eagles' runs carried their own built-in answers: quarterback read keeps, RPO tags, and a mix of schemes and directions, so a defense that loaded up for
"run" still had to guess where.

**What to notice:** a tendency costs you only if the defense can do something with it. Knowing the run is coming
helps a defense that can win at the line; it doesn't help much against a line and a back that win anyway. A
self-scout doesn't break every tendency. It asks which ones the next opponent can actually exploit, and spends
its tendency breakers there.
:::

### Does breaking a tendency pay?

If tendencies help defenses, then plays that go *against* the look should do better than plays that go with it.
The data lets you test that directly. Sort every neutral snap from 2022 to 2025 by what its look said (from the
team's other games, as above): "run" if the team passed less than 45% of the time from that look, "pass" if more
than 55%. Then compare what happened when the offense did what the look said, and when it didn't.

```{python}
#| label: fig-breaker-value
#| fig-cap: "Does going against the look pay? NFL neutral-situation snaps, 2022–2025 regular seasons. Left: expected points added (EPA) per play, by what the team's look said from its other games ('run' below a 45% pass rate, 'pass' above 55%) and what the offense actually did. A pass from a look that usually means run was worth about twice as much as a pass from a passing look; a run from a passing look was worth no more than a run from a running look. Right: the pass rows split by play-action. Without a run fake, a pass gained the same from either kind of look; with one, both did well. Passes from run looks were mostly play-action (the share is printed on each bar), and that explains their edge. Whiskers are 95% confidence intervals; the no-fake bar for run looks rests on few snaps, so its wide whisker means 'about the same' is a loose statement for that bar. Data: nflverse play-by-play, participation and FTN charting; course calculation."
style.apply()
fig, (a1, a2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.6, 3.1), sharex=False)
rows = [("run", "Look said run"), ("pass", "Look said pass")]
y = np.arange(2)
for off, did, col, lab in ((-0.18, 1, style.SERIES[0], "offense passed"), (0.18, 0, style.SERIES[1], "offense ran")):
    m = [BRK.loc[(s, did), "mean"] for s, _ in rows]
    e = [1.96 * BRK.loc[(s, did), "se"] for s, _ in rows]
    a1.barh(y + off, m, height=0.34, color=col, label=lab, zorder=3)
    a1.errorbar(m, y + off, xerr=e, fmt="none", ecolor=style.INK_2, elinewidth=0.9, capsize=2, zorder=4)
a1.axvline(0, color=style.BASELINE, lw=0.9)
a1.set_yticks(y, [t for _, t in rows], fontsize=7.6); a1.invert_yaxis()
a1.set_xlabel("EPA per play", fontsize=8); a1.tick_params(axis="x", labelsize=7.5)
a1.grid(axis="y", visible=False); a1.set_xlim(-0.12, 0.17)
a1.legend(loc="upper center", bbox_to_anchor=(0.45, -0.30), ncol=2, fontsize=7, frameon=False)
a1.set_title("All plays", fontsize=9.5)
for off, pa, col, lab in ((-0.18, True, style.SERIES[2], "play-action"), (0.18, False, style.MUTED, "no run fake")):
    m = [PA_SPLIT.loc[(s, pa), "mean"] for s, _ in rows]
    e = [1.96 * PA_SPLIT.loc[(s, pa), "se"] for s, _ in rows]
    a2.barh(y + off, m, height=0.34, color=col, label=lab, zorder=3)
    a2.errorbar(m, y + off, xerr=e, fmt="none", ecolor=style.INK_2, elinewidth=0.9, capsize=2, zorder=4)
for i, (s, _) in enumerate(rows):
    a2.text(0.205, i, f"{PA_SHARE[s]:.0%} of these\npasses were PA", fontsize=6.6, color=style.INK_2,
            va="center", ha="left")
a2.axvline(0, color=style.BASELINE, lw=0.9)
a2.set_yticks(y, [t for _, t in rows], fontsize=7.6); a2.invert_yaxis()
a2.set_xlabel("EPA per dropback", fontsize=8); a2.tick_params(axis="x", labelsize=7.5)
a2.grid(axis="y", visible=False); a2.set_xlim(0, 0.30)
a2.legend(loc="upper center", bbox_to_anchor=(0.45, -0.30), ncol=2, fontsize=7, frameon=False)
a2.set_title("The passes, split by play-action", fontsize=9.5)
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=1.2)
plt.show()
```

The left panel of @fig-breaker-value is half a yes. When the look said run and the offense threw, the pass was
worth `{python} f"{BRK.loc[('run', 1), 'mean']:+.2f}"` EPA on average, against
`{python} f"{BRK.loc[('pass', 1), 'mean']:+.2f}"` for passes from passing looks. Breaking a run tendency with a pass
paid. Breaking a pass tendency with a run did not: runs were worth about the same
(`{python} f"{BRK.loc[('pass', 0), 'mean']:+.2f}"` and `{python} f"{BRK.loc[('run', 0), 'mean']:+.2f}"`) whatever
the look said.

The right panel shows why. Split the passes by whether they started with a run fake, and the difference between
the looks disappears: a dropback without a fake was worth about the same from a running look as from a passing
look, and a play-action pass did well from both. What made passes from run looks better is that
`{python} pct(PA_SHARE['run'])` of them were play-action, against `{python} pct(PA_SHARE['pass'])` from passing
looks. In other words, the profitable tendency breaker in the NFL is not "surprise, it's a pass." It's "surprise,
it's a pass *that looks like the run you expected*." That's constraint theory and the illusion of complexity again,
showing up in the averages.

Treat this as what it is, an average over four seasons and every team, not a controlled experiment. Coaches choose
when to break tendencies, and they pick good moments, so some of the gain is selection. But the asymmetry is
striking, and it fits what coaches say: the run-look pass is the tendency breaker worth having.

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: Detroit Lions 2022–2024 — Ben Johnson's sequencing"}
Ben Johnson called Detroit's plays for three seasons, and by 2024 the Lions were the NFL's highest-scoring
offense.[^lions24] His offense was built from the Shanahan-family ingredients in this chapter, under-center
runs and play-action from the same looks, plus a taste for tendency breakers. The clearest example was the
sixth offensive lineman. Detroit was one of the league's heaviest users of a "jumbo" package with an extra lineman,
a look that tells most defenses "run": league-wide, offenses passed on about `{python} pct(NFL_J_PASS)` of neutral
snaps from it in 2022–2024. Detroit passed on `{python} pct(DET_J_PASS)` of its `{python} DET_J_N` neutral jumbo
snaps in those seasons, and `{python} pct(DET_J_PA)` of those passes were play-action: a run look hiding exactly the
kind of pass @fig-breaker-value found profitable. The most famous jumbo snap was the extreme version of the breaker. In a
December 2023 game at Dallas the Lions tried to take the lead on a two-point pass to a tackle, Taylor Decker, from
a heavy look that screams run; the officials ruled that the wrong tackle had reported as eligible, and the play was
wiped out.[^lionstwo]

**What to notice:** watch the snap *after* a Lions-style big run from under center. The offense knows the
defense's coaches have just told it to come up and stop the run, and that's the moment the same look turns into
play-action. Johnson took the approach with him to Chicago as head coach in 2025, where the Bears were second in
the league in play-action rate (see [04-05](../04-the-passing-game/04-05-play-action-boots-screens.qmd)) and,
in @fig-look-predictability, among the harder offenses to read.
:::

## The defense's version: one look, several answers

Defenses play the same game from the other side. A defense has base calls too, the coverage and front it wants to
be good at and calls most, and its own constraint plays: the blitz that punishes an offense for holding the ball (long
play-action shots, slow-developing dropbacks, a protection that always slides the same way), and the drop that
punishes a quarterback who expects a blitz and throws hot. It has tendencies the
offense's quality control coaches are hunting (does it blitz on third-and-medium? does the safety rotate toward
the motion?), and it self-scouts and breaks them too.

The defensive form of the illusion of complexity is the one you met in
[Disguise, Rotation and Split-Field](../06-pass-coverage/06-06-disguise-rotation-and-split-field.qmd) and
[Zone Blitzes and Simulated Pressure](../07-pressure/07-03-zone-blitz-and-simulated-pressure.qmd): show one
picture before the snap and play several things after it. The offense has to decide its protection and its hot
throws from the picture, so a picture that carries several defenses turns every one of those decisions into a guess.

Read @fig-one-look-three-answers, below, as a constraint tree turned around. The defense's base threat here is the
[Cover 0](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-cover-0) blitz: six rushers, as many as the offense can block even
with the back staying in, and nobody deep, so one missed assignment is a free rusher and the quarterback must
get the ball out right now, often hot, to whoever the blitz left uncovered.

Count the threats in its top-left panel. Four linemen, two mugged linebackers and two walked-up defenders make
eight possible rushers, and the offense has six blockers: five linemen and the back. It cannot block all eight, and
it doesn't try. That is the point of the look. The offense has to guess which six are coming, block those, and
have a hot throw ready for anyone extra. An offense that has seen the Cover 0 version a few times learns to answer
the [pressure look](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-pressure-look) the standard way: the quarterback identifies
the Mike, the center and the back take the two mugged linebackers, and the quarterback is "hot" off any seventh
rusher, throwing quick to the receiver that rusher left.

```{python}
#| label: fig-one-look-three-answers
#| fig-cap: "The defense's version: one pressure look, three answers (illustrative). Top left, the look: both linebackers mugged in the A gaps and the nickel ($) and strong safety (SS) walked up beside the ends (dashed rings: all four are blitz threats), so eight defenders could rush against six blockers, with one deep safety. A: Cover 0, six rush (the four linemen and both mugged linebackers) and everyone else plays man (dotted lines), nobody deep; the free safety comes down late to take the back. B: a fire zone, five rush, including the nickel off the edge, while the left end (purple ring) drops into a short zone: three deep, three under. C: simulated pressure, four rush (one of them the Mike), the Will and the right defensive tackle (purple rings) drop, seven cover. The protection has to be set, and the hot throw chosen, before the offense knows which one is coming."
LAT, WIN = (-14.4, 14.4), (-8.8, 18.6)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(6.2, 5.6))
ax = axes.flat
THREATS = ("MIKE", "WILL", "NB", "SS")
p = Play(spread(), mug_look(), los=35, to_go=None)
f = draw(p, ax=ax[0], lateral=LAT, window=WIN)
threat(f, p, *THREATS)
panel_title(ax[0], "The look: eight could rush, one deep")
say(f, p, -4.6, 8.0, "who rushes?\nwho drops?", fontsize=6.8, color=style.DEFENSE_DARK)
p = Play(spread(), mug_look(), los=35, to_go=None)
for k in ("LDE", "LDT", "RDT", "RDE", "MIKE", "WILL"):
    p.rush(k)
p.man("LCB", "X"); p.man("RCB", "Z"); p.man("NB", "H"); p.man("SS", "Y")
go_to(p, "FS", (5.5, -1.6), "path"); p.man("FS", "RB")
f = draw(p, ax=ax[1], lateral=LAT, window=WIN)
panel_title(ax[1], "A. Cover 0: 6 rush, man behind")
p = Play(spread(), mug_look(), los=35, to_go=None)
for k in ("NB", "LDT", "RDT", "RDE", "MIKE"):
    p.rush(k)
p.drop("LDE", (5.0, -5.0), zone=(4, 5)); p.drop("WILL", (6.0, 0.5), zone=(4, 5)); p.drop("SS", (6.0, 8.0), zone=(4, 5))
p.drop("LCB", (14.0, -10.0), zone=(5, 7)); p.drop("FS", (14.5, 0.0), zone=(5, 7))
p.drop("RCB", (14.0, 10.0), zone=(5, 7))
p.highlight("LDE", color=PURPLE)
f = draw(p, ax=ax[2], lateral=LAT, window=WIN)
panel_title(ax[2], "B. Fire zone: 5 rush, 3 deep, 3 under")
p = Play(spread(), mug_look(), los=35, to_go=None)
for k in ("LDE", "RDE", "LDT", "MIKE"):
    p.rush(k)
p.drop("WILL", (6.0, -4.0), zone=(4, 4)); p.drop("RDT", (5.5, 3.5), zone=(4, 4))
p.drop("NB", (5.0, -9.5), zone=(4, 4)); p.drop("SS", (5.0, 9.5), zone=(4, 4))
p.drop("LCB", (14.0, -10.0), zone=(5, 7)); p.drop("FS", (14.5, 0.0), zone=(5, 7))
p.drop("RCB", (14.0, 10.0), zone=(5, 7))
p.highlight("WILL", "RDT", color=PURPLE)
f = draw(p, ax=ax[3], lateral=LAT, window=WIN)
panel_title(ax[3], "C. Simulated pressure: 4 rush, 7 drop")
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=0.5, h_pad=0.7)
plt.show()
```

The
[fire zone](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-fire-zone) and the
[simulated pressure](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-simulated-pressure) are the defense's constraint plays
against *that* answer. They drop players into the windows where the hot throws go and bring rushers from where the
protection isn't looking, so the offense's answer to the blitz becomes the defense's opportunity.

The same structure holds for coverage shells. A two-high shell that can rotate to Cover 3 at the snap, or a
single-high look that spins back to two deep, is one picture carrying several coverages, and it constrains the
quarterback's pre-snap read the way a run-and-boot look constrains a linebacker's first step. The defenses that
lean hardest on this, such as Brian Flores's Vikings in 06-06's film room, are the hardest to scout, because
their tendencies are built to be coin flips.

The defense also has to self-scout. A defense that always rotates the safety toward the motion, or always blitzes
on third-and-6, has handed the offense a free play: motion to set the rotation, or a screen against the blitz.
The cure is the same as on offense: break it, hide it, or keep it as bait for one big moment.

::: {.callout-tip title="Watch for it on Sunday: call the follow-up"}
Pick one offense for a quarter and keep a tiny log: the look (personnel and where the quarterback stands)
and the play.

**Before the snap**

- Is this a look you've already seen today? Say what it was used for last time.
- If the last play from this look was a big run, say "play-action" out loud. It's the most common follow-up in
  football, usually within the next few snaps.
- Pick out the cheater: the linebacker flowing early, the backside end crashing down the line instead of
  squeezing, the safety creeping down. The next constraint play will be aimed at him.

**After the snap**

- First step: did the line go the same way as the base play? If so, watch the ball, not the line.
- Did the ball come back against the flow (counter), the quarterback roll away from it (boot), or the throw go
  over the safety who came down (shot)? Name the defender it punished.
- On defense: when you see a pressure look on third down, count rushers at the snap. If a mugged linebacker
  drops, you've seen the defense's constraint play against the hot throw.
:::

## Predict the play

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play 1: the flow and the end"}
```{python}
#| label: fig-predict-flow
#| fig-cap: "Second-and-6, second quarter. The offense is back in its favorite look: 21 personnel, offset I, tight end right. The faint dashed arrows show what the defense did on the offense's last three outside-zone runs to the right from this look: both linebackers flew to the play side at the snap, while the backside end (ringed) now plays boot, counter, reverse: he squeezes the cutback a yard down the line but keeps his shoulders square and his eyes on the quarterback, instead of crashing down the line as he did earlier in the game."
p = Play(offset_i(), base_43(), los=45, to_go=6)
f = draw(p, lateral=(-13, 13), window=(-8.6, 15.5), width_in=5.4)
ghost(f, p, [(4.6, 1.0), (3.9, 2.6), (3.0, 4.2)], alpha=0.8, lw=1.6)
ghost(f, p, [(4.6, -2.6), (5.3, -0.6), (5.2, 2.8)], alpha=0.8, lw=1.6)
ghost(f, p, [(0.3, -4.5), (-0.5, -2.7)], color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, alpha=1.0, lw=1.8, zorder=9)
cx, cy = _P(f, p, 1.0, technique("5", -1))
f.ax.add_patch(Circle((float(cx), float(cy)), 1.05, fc="none", ec=RED, lw=1.7, zorder=7))
point_to(f, p, (10.8, -5.6), (5.1, -1.4), "last three runs:\nlinebackers fly right", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK)
point_to(f, p, (-4.8, -8.4), (-0.1, -3.4), "end squeezes a yard,\neyes on Q (no chase)", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK)
plt.show()
```

**The defense has adjusted to the outside zone and to the boot. What does the offense call, and where does the
ball go?**

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**A counter to the left (or another run back against the flow), not the naked boot.** Two things have changed.
The linebackers are flowing even harder, which is the counter's cue: it starts like outside zone and brings the
ball back to the side they just left. And the backside end has stopped crashing. He now plays boot, counter,
reverse: he squeezes a yard, keeps his eyes on the quarterback and stays at the edge. That kills the naked boot,
because he is standing on the spot the quarterback would roll to, facing him.

Is the end a problem for the counter, too? Partly: a disciplined boot-counter-reverse end is also a counter
defender (it's the C in his checklist). But a squeezing end is exactly the man the pulling guard is built to kick
out, and the guard comes at him from inside, with a good angle. (If he squeezes so hard that he crosses the guard's
face, the guard logs him, sealing him inside, and the back bends outside instead.) The counter still wins here
because the *linebackers'* over-flow is the bigger cheat, and nothing else on the tree punishes it as directly.
Expect the back to take one step right, then the right guard (or the tight end, in some versions) to pull back
across, kick the end out, and the fullback to lead up onto the Will, who has to stop, turn and come back.

What about the protected bootleg, branch (1) on the tree? The linebackers are flying, and it puts a blocker on the
end, so it's a reasonable second answer, and partial credit if you said it. It is worse than the counter here
because of where this end is: he is waiting at the quarterback's launch point with his eyes on the quarterback, so
the boot's lone blocker meets a defender who expects him, the quarterback has to pull up early, and the crossing
routes don't get time to come open behind the linebackers.

If you said "naked boot," that was the right answer a few snaps ago, when the end was crashing. The tree in
@fig-constraint-tree is a map of *which* defender to punish; this defense moved, so the answer moved with it. If the
end starts crashing again, the naked boot comes back.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play 2: right after the big run"}
```{python}
#| label: fig-predict-after-run
#| fig-cap: "First-and-10 at the opponent's 38, early in the third quarter. Two snaps ago, from this exact look (12 personnel, under center, both tight ends attached to the line), the offense ran outside zone for 23 yards. In its neutral-situation film this season the offense has passed on about 30% of its snaps from this look. The defense has brought its strong safety (SS, ringed) down to about seven yards, and the free safety is the only deep defender."
def ace_12():
    return line() + [O("QB", "QB", -1.9, 0.0, "Q"), O("RB", "RB", -7.0, 0.0, "R"), O("Y", "TE", -0.7, 4.8, "Y"),
                     O("U", "TE", -0.7, -4.8, "U"), O("X", "WR", -1.5, -11.0, "X"), O("Z", "WR", -1.5, 11.0, "Z")]


dfn = [q.moved(d=1.0, w=-5.7) if q.key == "WDE" else q for q in base_43()]
dfn = [q.moved(d=6.8, w=4.0) if q.key == "SS" else q for q in dfn]
dfn = [q.moved(w=-11.0) if q.key == "LCB" else (q.moved(w=11.0) if q.key == "RCB" else q) for q in dfn]
p = Play(ace_12(), dfn, los=72, to_go=10)
p.highlight("SS", color=RED)
f = draw(p, lateral=(-14.5, 14.5), window=(-8.6, 16.5), width_in=5.4)
say(f, p, 13.0, 4.0, "one deep", fontsize=6.8, color=style.DEFENSE_DARK)
plt.show()
```

**Run or pass? If pass, what kind, and what is the defense afraid of?**

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**This is the snap for a play-action shot, and if it's a pass it's likely to go deep, though run is still the
single most likely call.** Start with the numbers: from this look the offense passes about three times
in ten, so a pure tendency guess says run. That's what the defense's tendency report says too, and after a 23-yard
run its coaches will have told it to stop the run, which is why the strong safety has come down to seven yards.
That's the lean.

Now think like the play-caller. The best time to break a tendency is when the defense is most committed to it.
A play-action shot from the same look, with the same line steps and the same back's track, attacks the one deep
safety: one receiver deep down the middle to hold him, another on a deep crossing route behind the linebackers who
come forward on the fake, seven or eight players blocking. @fig-breaker-value is the case for it: passes from looks
that usually mean run have been worth about twice as much as ordinary passes, almost entirely because they're
play-action.

A good defense knows this too, which is why many coordinators keep a safety deep for a snap or two after a big run
even when the scouting report says run. That matters for the offense in two ways. If the quarterback has a
check at the line and sees the defense back out of the eight-man look before the snap (the strong safety drifting
back to two deep), he can check to the run, because the shot has lost its target. And if the defense disguises it
and the free safety bails at the snap, the shot is covered on this play, but the offense has learned something
for the next snap from this look: a defense that is guarding the deep middle has fewer men in the box, and the
run is back on.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play 3: the third time they show it"}
```{python}
#| label: fig-predict-mug
#| fig-cap: "Third-and-7. The defense shows the same pressure look for the third time today: both linebackers mugged in the A gaps and the nickel and strong safety walked up beside the ends (dashed rings: blitz threats), one deep safety. The first two times it was a six-man Cover 0 blitz, and both times the quarterback beat it with a quick throw to the slot receiver on his left (H), right where a blitzing Will had come from."
p = Play(spread(), mug_look(), los=40, to_go=7)
f = draw(p, lateral=(-14.6, 14.6), window=(-7.6, 15.5), width_in=5.6)
threat(f, p, "MIKE", "WILL", "NB", "SS")
ghost(f, p, [(-1.0, -7.3), (1.0, -6.0), (4.2, -2.9)], color=style.OFFENSE, alpha=0.7)
point_to(f, p, (11.0, -6.0), (4.0, -3.2), "where the hot throw\nwent twice", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK)
plt.show()
```

**Six rushers again? What should the quarterback expect?**

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**Probably not six this time: expect a simulated pressure or a fire zone, with a defender dropping into H's
window.** The defense's base threat has been beaten twice in the same way: the offense now expects six, puts the
center and the back on the two mugged linebackers and throws hot to the slot. That answer is exactly what the defense's constraint plays
are built to punish. The likeliest call drops one of the mugged linebackers (most likely the Will, on H's side)
straight into the short window the hot throw has been going to, and brings a rusher from somewhere the protection
isn't looking, such as the nickel off the edge (he's walked up, so he can) or a lineman looping. Four or five rush; six or seven cover.

For the quarterback, the danger is throwing the same hot route on rhythm into a defender who is waiting for it.
The better plan is to hold the ball a beat to see who actually comes, or to have a route behind the dropper. The
defense can also bluff the other way and blitz six a third time, betting that the offense has adjusted already;
that's the coin flip the defense wants the quarterback to face. But after two clean hot completions, the
sequencing logic points to the drop.
:::
:::

## Takeaways

- **Base plays are what an offense wants to be good at; constraint plays punish the defense for stopping them.**
  Every constraint play is defined by the defender it punishes: find the defender who is cheating and you've found
  the play that's coming.
- **The two need each other.** The base play keeps the defense leaning, the constraint plays limit the lean, and a
  constraint play's average *should* look better than the base play's even when it's called the right amount,
  because each extra call costs a little on every other snap.
- **The illusion of complexity works from both ends.** One play in many outfits gives the defense more to prepare;
  many plays from one look gives it nothing to read. Both hide tells.
- **Sequencing is the order of the conversation:** the counter after the flow, play-action after the big run, the
  tendency breaker after a stretch of predictability. Sometimes the right follow-up is the same play again.
- **Tendencies are real and measurable.** In neutral situations from 2022 to 2025, personnel plus the quarterback's
  alignment called about two snaps in three correctly; the hardest offenses to read came mostly from the Shanahan
  family of offenses. Passes from run looks paid off, mostly because they were play-action.
- **Defenses play the same game:** one pressure look or one shell carrying several calls, and their own self-scout.
