[^brownct]: The idea is much older than the name; the name "constraint theory" was popularized by the coach and writer
    Chris B. Brown on his Smart Football site, for example in "Why Every Team Should Apply the Constraint Theory of
    Offense" (June 14, 2011), which separates an offense's "base, core plays" from the "constraint plays" (bubble screens,
    play-action, bootlegs, draws, traps) that make defenders "pay for their impatience" when they cheat:
    <https://web.archive.org/web/20110616214847/http://smartfootball.com/offense/why-every-team-should-apply-the-constraint-theory-of-offense>.

[^minimax]: The textbook game-theory version says something different: if both sides choose at random each snap
    and neither can learn from the other's history, the offense's best mix makes its plays equally valuable *on average*.
    Brian Burke laid out that argument for run-pass balance in "Game Theory and Run/Pass Balance," Advanced NFL Stats,
    June 13, 2008:
    <https://web.archive.org/web/20080920054748/http://www.advancednflstats.com/2008/06/game-theory-and-runpass-balance.html>.
    The toy model here lets the defense *learn* how often the constraint comes from film, which is what leaves a gap in
    the averages. Which picture fits real play-calling better is exactly what the economists argue about.

[^illusion]: The phrase is common shorthand in the Shanahan family of offenses, and its first use is not well documented.
    Robert Mays used it of Kyle Shanahan's Falcons offense in "The NFL's Newest Mastermind Eyes the Throne," The Ringer,
    Jan. 30, 2017: <https://www.theringer.com/2017/01/30/nfl/kyle-shanahan-atlanta-falcons-super-bowl-nfl-playoffs-4a40f26c05e2>.
    Matt LaFleur used it on taking the Packers job in January 2019; Davante Adams said LaFleur "wants to bring in a new kind
    of innovative style -- an illusion of complexity" (Rob Demovsky, ESPN, Jan. 28, 2019:
    <https://www.espn.com/blog/green-bay-packers/post/_/id/46765/davante-adams-packers-offense-will-be-new-school-under-new-coach>).
    Later profiles trace the phrase to the Washington staff (2010s) that included Kyle Shanahan, LaFleur and Sean McVay.

[^motion]: Daire Carragher, "NFL pre-snap motion usage reaches new highs across the NFL," PFF, Feb. 23, 2026 (shift or
    motion on 38.4% of plays in 2016 and 63.9% in 2025): <https://www.pff.com/news/nfl-pre-snap-motion-usage-reaches-new-highs-across-the-nfl>.
    PFF's series counts shifts as well as motion and is not comparable with FTN's `is_motion` flag.

[^rams18]: Course calculation from nflverse participation data, 2018 regular season, runs and passes with a recorded
    personnel grouping: the Rams were in 11 personnel on 92.7% of plays (about 1,040 plays); the median team was at about
    65% and the next-highest team, Green Bay, at 76%.

[^raymond]: Raymond's line is quoted in Chris B. Brown, "The Making of a Modern-Day Guru," Grantland, January 3, 2014:
    <https://grantland.com/features/gus-malzahn-offensive-evolution/>. See also Harold R. Raymond and Ted Kempski, *The
    Delaware Wing-T: An Order of Football* (Parker Publishing, 1986).

[^walsh]: Bill Walsh with Brian Billick and James Peterson, *Finding the Winning Edge* (Sports Publishing, 1998), on scripting
    the opening plays; AP obituary via NFL.com (July 30, 2007), crediting Walsh with popularizing "the practice of scripting
    the first 15 offensive plays of a game": <https://www.nfl.com/news/hall-of-fame-coach-bill-walsh-who-won-three-super-bowls-with-th-09000d5d800879e1>.
    Accounts of the script's length range from 15 to about 25 plays.

[^levitt]: Kenneth Kovash and Steven D. Levitt, "Professionals Do Not Play Minimax: Evidence from Major League Baseball and
    the National Football League," NBER Working Paper 15347 (September 2009): <https://www.nber.org/papers/w15347>. They report
    negative serial correlation in NFL run-pass choices (teams switch more than an unpredictable mix would: other things
    equal, a team that has just passed is about 10 percentage points less likely to pass next) and argue that teams passed
    too rarely in the seasons studied (2001–2005); summary in the NBER Digest, October 2009:
    <https://www.nber.org/digest/oct09/w15347.html>.

[^selfscout]: For example, Titans coach Mike Munchak on his staff's 2012 bye week: "see what our tendencies are ... how
    other teams look at us as an offense, defense, special teams" ("Titans Coaches Using Bye to Scout Own Team,"
    TennesseeTitans.com, Nov. 13, 2012: <https://www.tennesseetitans.com/news/titans-coaches-using-bye-to-scout-own-team-8831526>);
    and Matt LaFleur's 2019 Packers, whose offensive and defensive staffs studied each other's side of the ball over the
    bye for "a different perspective of how opponents would attack one side of the ball, where we think there could be
    holes or potential holes" (Mike Spofford, "Packers taking hard look at themselves over the bye,"
    Packers.com, Nov. 11, 2019: <https://www.packers.com/news/packers-taking-hard-look-at-themselves-over-the-bye>).

[^corndog]: "Corn Dog (American football)," *Wikipedia*: <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corn_Dog_(American_football)> (Toney
    5-yard touchdown at 12:04 and Moore 4-yard touchdown at 9:22 of the fourth quarter; the Super Bowl LVIII version, renamed
    "Tom and Jerry," for Mecole Hardman's walk-off touchdown); Super Bowl LVII result, Kansas City 38, Philadelphia 35
    (Feb. 12, 2023): <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_Bowl_LVII>.

[^neutral]: Method for every chart in this section: nflverse play-by-play (`load_pbp`) joined to participation
    (`load_participation`, for personnel) and FTN charting (`load_ftn_charting`, for the quarterback's alignment: `qb_location`
    U, S or P), regular seasons 2022–2025. Neutral = first or second down, win probability 0.20–0.80, more than two minutes
    left in the half. Personnel = backs (RB + FB) then tight ends. "Pass" = nflverse's `pass` flag, so sacks and scrambles
    count as passes. The predictions use only the team's other games in the same season (a look needed at least eight snaps
    elsewhere; otherwise the team's overall rate was used). Participation data for 2023 onward comes from FTN and earlier
    seasons from NGS, so personnel is coded differently across the 2022/2023 break; the backs-and-tight-ends count used
    here is unaffected. A sixth offensive lineman is not counted as a tight end here, so "jumbo" snaps fall into 11 or
    12 personnel; that is about 3% of neutral snaps league-wide in 2024 and about 7% of Detroit's (28 of 418, mostly coded
    12), too few to move the tables. The Lions film room counts those jumbo snaps separately (six or more offensive
    linemen in the participation data). RPOs are coded by what happened, so an RPO that ended in a handoff is a run;
    that pushes RPO-heavy offenses' looks toward whichever answer they chose after the snap, and is one more reason to
    read the hit rates as rough.

[^afterrun]: Course calculation from nflverse play-by-play and FTN charting (`is_play_action`), 2022–2025 regular
    seasons, neutral first-and-10 dropbacks that were not the first play of a drive. "Right after a big run" means the
    previous snap of the same drive was a run that gained 10 or more yards. Comparing only first-and-10 snaps keeps the
    down and distance the same, since a big run usually ends in a fresh first down.

[^jets]: Associated Press, "Jets hire Tanner Engstrand as offensive coordinator and Chris Banjo as special teams
    coordinator" (Feb. 1, 2025), which describes Engstrand as the Lions' passing game coordinator:
    <https://www.news4jax.com/sports/2025/02/01/jets-hire-tanner-engstrand-as-offensive-coordinator-and-chris-banjo-as-special-teams-coordinator/>.
    The Jets' offensive coordinator for 2026 is Frank Reich (course fact sheet).

[^barkley]: Pro Football Reference, Saquon Barkley (2,005 rushing yards in 2024): <https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/B/BarkSa00.htm>;
    Super Bowl LIX, Feb. 9, 2025: Philadelphia 40, Kansas City 22 (course fact sheet). The pistol figures are a course
    calculation (method in the note on neutral situations).

[^lions24]: Detroit went 15–2 in 2024 and led the NFL with 564 points (33.2 a game): Pro Football Reference, 2024 Detroit Lions:
    <https://www.pro-football-reference.com/teams/det/2024.htm>. Johnson was Detroit's offensive coordinator from 2022 to
    2024 and became the Bears' head coach in 2025 (course fact sheet). Points and record also check against nflverse
    schedules (564 points in 17 games; Buffalo next with 525).

[^lionstwo]: Detroit at Dallas, Dec. 30, 2023 (Week 17), Cowboys 20, Lions 19. After the game referee Brad Allen said in a pool
    report that No. 70 (Dan Skipper), not No. 68 (Decker), had reported as eligible; see "2023 Detroit Lions season,"
    Wikipedia: <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Detroit_Lions_season>, and Associated Press, "Lions take issue with
    officials after potential winning 2-point pass is negated by penalty" (Dec. 31, 2023):
    <https://www.ksat.com/sports/2023/12/31/lions-take-issue-with-officials-after-potential-winning-2-point-pass-is-negated-by-penalty/>.
    Detroit's sixth-lineman share (9.8% of runs and passes in 2022, second to Cleveland) is from
    [Personnel Groupings](../02-personnel-and-formations/02-01-personnel-groupings.qmd).
